title: Set Operations
story: Your music app needs to filter playlists. You have a Set of your favorite artists and a Set of artists on a festival lineup. You need to find which of your favorites are playing — and which artists are on the lineup that you haven't discovered yet.
why: Set operations — insert, contains, remove, plus logical combinations — model real-world filtering and membership scenarios.
analogy: Set operations are like a bouncer at a club with a guest list. `.insert()` adds names to the list. `.contains()` checks 'Are you on the list?' before letting someone in. `.remove()` crosses a name off. The duplicate detection pattern is like checking 'Have I seen this person before?' before writing their name down again.
try_it: Implement an intersection function: given two Sets, return a Set of elements that are in BOTH. Implement a union function: return a Set of elements in EITHER. Test both with the festival example — which artists are in both your list and the lineup (intersection), and what's the complete combined list (union)?
tips: Use a Set to track 'seen' items when scanning a Vec — it's the fastest way to detect duplicates
`.contains()` is O(1) — just as fast as Map lookup, regardless of Set size
When you need both membership testing AND counting, use Map instead — Set only tracks presence
common_mistakes: Checking for duplicates by scanning the whole Vec for each element — that's O(n^2); use a Set for O(n)
Using Set when you need a COUNT of how many times something appeared — Set doesn't store counts
Forgetting that `.remove()` returns Bool — `true` means 'I found and removed it', `false` means 'wasn't there'
